This passage is from **Homer's *Iliad*, Book 19, lines 184–197**. It occurs during the reconciliation scene where Agamemnon responds to Odysseus' advice, agrees to swear an oath that he has not touched Briseis, and orders the promised gifts to be brought to Achilles.

Here is a line-by-line English translation, keeping close to the original syntax and Homeric tone:

> Then in reply spoke Agamemnon, lord of men:  
> “I am glad, son of Laertes, having heard your words,  
> for you have set forth and recounted everything in due measure.  
> These things I am willing to swear, and my heart commands me,  
> nor will I swear falsely before the gods. But let Achilles  
> wait there for now, though he is eager for battle;  
> and do you all others wait here assembled, until the gifts  
> come from my tent and we swear binding oaths.  
> To you yourself I give this charge and command:  
> choose out the noblest young men of all the Achaeans  
> to bring from my ship the gifts, all that we  
> promised yesterday to give to Achilles, and to bring the women.  
> And let Talthybius quickly, throughout the broad camp of the Achaeans,  
> prepare a boar to sacrifice to Zeus and the Sun.”

### 🔍 Translation Notes & Homeric Idioms:
- **Λαερτιάδη**: "Son of Laertes" = Odysseus. Homer frequently uses patronymics.
- **ἐν μοίρῃ ... διίκεο καὶ κατέλεξας**: Literally "you have gone through and recounted in due portion." Refers to Odysseus having spoken properly and in correct order.
- **πρὸς δαίμονος**: "Before the divine power/gods." Agamemnon is emphasizing the sacredness of the oath he is about to take.
- **ὅρκια πιστὰ τάμωμεν**: Literally "cut faithful oaths." In Greek ritual, oaths were ratified by cutting (τάμνειν) the throats of sacrificial animals. Hence, "swear binding/solemn oaths."
- **ἐπειγόμενός περ Ἄρηος**: "Though eager for Ares (i.e., battle)." Ares is commonly used metonymically for war.
- **κάπρον ... ταμέειν Διί τ᾽ Ἠελίῳ τε**: The boar is prepared for the oath-sacrifice. Zeus and Helios (the Sun) are invoked as witnesses because they see and oversee all human actions and oaths.

This passage marks a pivotal moment in the *Iliad*: the formal end of the quarrel between Agamemnon and Achilles, clearing the way for Achilles' return to battle. Let me know if you'd like a metrical analysis, vocabulary breakdown, or comparison with other English translations.

Here is a line-by-line English translation, keeping close to the original syntax and Homeric tone:

> Then in reply spoke Agamemnon, lord of men:  
> “I am glad, son of Laertes, having heard your words,  
> for you have set forth and recounted everything in due measure.  
> These things I am willing to swear, and my heart commands me,  
> nor will I swear falsely before the gods. But let Achilles

> and do you all others wait here assembled, until the gifts

> choose out the noblest young men of all the Achaeans  
> to bring from my ship the gifts, all that we

> And let Talthybius quickly, throughout the broad camp of the Achaeans,  
> prepare a boar to sacrifice to Zeus and the Sun.”

### 🔍 Translation Notes & Homeric Idioms:
- **Λαερτιάδη**: "Son of Laertes" = Odysseus. Homer frequently uses patronymics.
- **ἐν μοίρῃ ... διίκεο καὶ κατέλεξας**: Literally "you have gone through and recounted in due portion." Refers to Odysseus having spoken properly and in correct order.
- **πρὸς δαίμονος**: "Before the divine power/gods." Agamemnon is emphasizing the sacredness of the oath he is about to take.
- **ὅρκια πιστὰ τάμωμεν**: Literally "cut faithful oaths." In Greek ritual, oaths were ratified by cutting (τάμνειν) the throats of sacrificial animals. Hence, "swear binding/solemn oaths."
- **ἐπειγόμενός περ Ἄρηος**: "Though eager for Ares (i.e., battle)." Ares is commonly used metonymically for war.
- **κάπρον ... ταμέειν Διί τ᾽ Ἠελίῳ τε**: The boar is prepared for the oath-sacrifice. Zeus and Helios (the Sun) are invoked as witnesses because they see and oversee all human actions and oaths.
